newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel tells Egypt will stick to peace pledges.
newsitem.headline: Israel tells Egypt will stick to peace pledges.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said his Israeli opposite number Ezer Weizman assured him on Monday that the Jewish state would abide by peace pledges it had signed with the Palestinians.
"The president assured me that they are honouring the agreements and it is going to be implemented," Mubarak told a joint news conference after two hours of talks with Weizman.
"I have the words from the president of Israel that Israel is honouring its commitment and is going to fulfill and implement the agreement," he added.

Weizman arrived in Cairo on a good will mission aimed at convincing a sceptical Egypt that his country is committed to peace despite demands by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to change parts of the agreements signed with the Palestinians.
Mubarak also said he will only meet Netanyahu after Israeli troops withdrew from the West Bank town of Hebron as stipulated by a peace deal signed previously.
The Israeli prime minister wants to change the conditions of the accord to guarantee security for the minority Jewish settlers living in Hebron.
The Palestinans are refusing point blank to open the issue for renegotiation and are accusing Netanyahu of reneging on peace deals.
"We have had security problems in the past and we hope that we will be over...the government is not going back," Weizman, whose role is largely ceremonial, told the news conference.

"The government has perhaps slowed down but I'm sure as I've said to President Mubarak that the government of Israel will continue and do all its best to achieve peace with the Palestinians," he said.

Netanyahu's hard line on deals signed with the Palestinians has brought Israel's relations with its neighbours to boiling point, even grating on the nerves of moderate Egypt -- the first Arab country to make peace with the Jewish state.

Weizman, an architect of the 1979 Egyptian-Israeli peace deal and a good friend of assassinated president Anwar Sadat, also has strong ties with Mubarak and analysts say he is well suited to tide over anger at Netanyahu's policies.
Mubarak has said Egyptians were furious at Netanyahu and that they were calling for a boycott of Israel but Weizman told reporters he had recommended a more pragmatic approach.

"He (Netanyahu) has difficulties because...the shooting that unfortunately took place and it's hampering a little with the atmosphere," Weizman said, referring to gun battles last month which killed more than 70 Arabs and Israelis.

"We have to overcome it...I am sure that Netanyahu wants just as much as all of us to achieve peace and security as much as possible. Therefore I recommended to the president that Netanyahu is a fact like it's been recommended to me that Arafat is a fact," he added.
Netanyahu's radical policies have galvanised Weizman into action rare in Israeli presidential history.

Mubarak, who refused to attend an emergency peace summit in Washington because of Netanyahu's policies, told reporters that he was not annoyed at the Israeli prime minister but inisted he would only meet him after the Hebron issue was settled.
"It is not a question of being upset or annoyed, its a matter of discussing how to push the process forward," he said.
"The problem is the redeployment from Hebron. Whenever they reach a solution to that I am ready to meet with him (Netanyahu) and I told him this in my last contact on the phone."
